instructions: The night before, or at least 4 hours ahead: Remove the stems from the ancho chiles, split them open and shake out the seeds. Toast them in a dry skillet over medium heat for about 20 seconds per side, until they smell fruity.
Transfer the chiles to a bowl, cover them with hot water and let them soak for 20 minutes, until soft.

Lift the chiles into a blender with a slotted spoon. Add the vinegar, garlic, 2 tsp salt, oregano, cumin and thyme. Blend into a thick, fairly smooth paste. If it won't blend, add 1 tbsp of the soaking water.
Pat the pork chops dry and spread the paste on both sides. Put them in a covered dish and refrigerate.

Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a large heavy skillet over medium heat. Cook the chops in two batches, 5 to 6 minutes per side, until they're deep red-brown. Add the other 1 tbsp oil for the second batch. You're cooking the pork to 145°F in the middle, so if you have a thermometer, check it there. No thermometer? Cut into the thickest chop. It's done when the juices run clear and the center is just barely blush pink.
Turn the heat to medium-high and brown each chop for about 30 seconds per side. Transfer the chops to a plate and let them rest for 5 minutes.
Meanwhile, thinly slice half the red onion and 4 radishes, and shred a few lettuce leaves.
Serve the chops with the sliced onion, lettuce and radishes.
advance_prep_notes: marinate at least 4 hours ahead (or overnight)
method_notes: Lead is Diana Kennedy's chuletas de puerco adobadas as printed on FoodGeeks (no ratings, so a fallback lead); the Jauja Cocina Mexicana version also has no ratings. Both make an adobo from soaked ancho chiles, garlic, spices and an acid (vinegar here, a sour orange mix in Jauja), marinate the chops, then cook them slowly on medium heat. The marinade is the advance step; it's the step that gives the dish its flavor. Boneless loin chops replace pounded shoulder chops, and vegetable oil replaces lard.
